R Lab: Data Structures - Matrix and Array
 
Part A — Creating Matrices
```{r}
m1 <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
m1
```
 
```{r}
m2 <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
m2
```
 
```{r}
scores <- matrix(c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84, 90), nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
rownames(scores) <- c("Quiz1", "Quiz2")
colnames(scores) <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid")
 
scores
```
Question #1
Answer: By default, R fills matrices column by column (equivalent to byrow = FALSE). Setting byrow = TRUE changes this behavior so that R fills the matrix row by row across each row before moving to the next.
 
m1 (byrow = FALSE): Fills down the first column first ($1, 2, 3$), then the second ($4, 5, 6$), and finally the third ($7, 8, 9$).
 
m2 (byrow = TRUE): Fills across the first row first ($1, 2, 3$), then the second row ($4, 5, 6$), and finally the third row ($7, 8, 9$).
 
Question #2
```{r}
matrix(1:8, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
```
Explanation:
R uses vector recycling when the input vector is shorter than the matrix size. Since the matrix requires 9 elements ($3 \times 3$) and only 8 are provided ($1$ to $8$), R recycles the first element ($1$) to fill the 9th slot in column 3.
 
Warning Message:
R will issue the following warning because the total number of matrix slots ($9$) is not a multiple of the input vector length ($8$):
 
Part B — Subsetting Matrices
```{r}
# Access the single value in row 1, column 2
scores[1, 2]
 
# Access the entire first row
scores[1, ]
 
# Access the entire "Ben" column
scores[, "Ben"]
```
 
```{r}
# Return values in scores greater than or equal to 90
scores[scores >= 90]
```
Question #3
R "downgrades" (or drops dimensions) a single row or column of a matrix to a 1D numeric vector (or class "numeric").
```{r}
class(scores[1, ])
# Output: "numeric"
 
class(scores[, "Ben"])
# Output: "numeric"
```
Why R Does This Automatically?
Answer: R has an automatic dimension-reduction behavior controlled by drop = TRUE (which is the default in [ matrix subsetting). When subsetting results in a single row or column, 2D matrix structure is no longer strictly necessary to represent the values, so R automatically flattens it into a simpler, memory-efficient 1D vector to simplify further vector operations.
 
 
Question #4
In the matrix-logical chunk, the row/column names disappeared from your result. * Why does subsetting with a logical condition (scores >= 90) lose the 2D shape and names thatscores[1, ] kept?
 
Answer:
Variable Result Length & Irregular Shape: A matrix requires a rigid rectangular grid (all rows must have the same number of columns). Logical indexing evaluates every single cell independently across the entire matrix. Because the elements matching scores >= 90 might come from arbitrary position combinations (e.g., 2 elements from row 1, 1 element from row 2), the extracted values cannot form a valid 2D matrix grid without leaving empty spaces.
 
Dimension-Specific Metadata: Matrix row names and column names belong to whole rows and whole columns (the 2D grid structure). When R collapses the extracted elements into a single 1D vector to fit the arbitrary number of matching items, the 2D matrix dimensions (dim) along with their associated rownames and colnames are discarded.
 
Part C — Matrix Properties and Operations
```{r}
# Report dimensions using dim(), nrow(), and ncol()
dim(scores)
nrow(scores)
ncol(scores)
 
# Transpose scores, store as scores_t, print scores_t and compare dimensions
scores_t <- t(scores)
scores_t
dim(scores_t)
```
 
```{r}
a <- matrix(1:4, nrow = 2)
b <- matrix(5:8, nrow = 2)
 
# Element-wise addition
a + b
 
# Element-wise multiplication
a * b
```
 
```{r}
# True matrix multiplication using %*%
a %*% b
```
Question #5
a * b and a %*% b both “multiply” the same two matrices but give different results.
Explain the difference between element-wise multiplication and matrix multiplication in your own words.
 
Answer: Element-wise Multiplication (a * b): Multiplies corresponding elements in the exact same positions. For example, the value at a[1,1] is multiplied directly by b[1,1], a[1,2] by b[1,2], and so on. Both matrices must have identical dimensions.
 
Matrix Multiplication (a %*% b): Follows linear algebra matrix multiplication rules. Each entry in the resulting matrix is calculated as the dot product of a row from matrix a and a column from matrix b (multiplying elements across the row by elements down the column and summing them up). For this to work, the number of columns in a must equal the number of rows in b.
 
Question #6
t(scores) swaps rows and columns. Look at dim(scores) versus dim(scores_t).
Why must the row/column names also swap positions when you transpose a matrix?
 
Answer:
Transposing a matrix using t() swaps rows and columns, including their names. This keeps the data correctly labeled, so each student’s quiz scores remain associated with the right student and quiz.
 
Part D — cbind() and rbind()
```{r}
# Add new column "Dex" to scores using cbind()
Dex <- c(85, 91)
scores_v2 <- cbind(scores, Dex)
scores_v2
```
 
```{r}
# Add new row "Quiz3" to scores using rbind()
Quiz3 <- c(80, 88, 93)
scores_v3 <- rbind(scores, Quiz3)
scores_v3
```
Question #7
```{r}
cbind(scores, c(85, 91, 100))
```
 
Answer: R will still execute the operation using vector recycling, but it will trigger a warning message because $3$ values cannot fit evenly into a $2$-row column:
 
Explanation:
cbind() combines objects column-by-column, meaning any new column must match the number of rows of the existing matrix.
 
rbind() combines objects row-by-row, meaning any new row must match the number of columns of the existing matrix.
 
Matching dimensions are required because a matrix is a rigid 2D grid structure. Every row must contain the exact same number of columns, and every column must contain the exact same number of rows.
 
Question #8
Answer:
When to use rbind() instead of cbind():
 
Use rbind() when you are adding new observations/records (rows) over time for an existing set of variables/features (columns). Conversely, cbind() is used when adding new attributes/variables for existing observation subjects.
 
Concrete Example:
Daily Sales Tracking: Each column represents fixed metrics—Date, Units_Sold, and Revenue. At the end of every business day, you log a new transaction record by appending a row to the dataset using rbind(). You use rbind() because the measured attributes stay constant, but the number of observed days increases over time.
 
Part E — Arrays: Creating and Subsetting
```{r}
# Create a 2x3x2 array called arr and print it
arr <- array(1:12, dim = c(2, 3, 2))
arr
```
 
```{r}
# Access element in row 1, column 2, of the SECOND layer
arr[1, 2, 2]
 
# Access the entire first layer (slice) of arr
arr[, , 1]
```
 
```{r}
# Confirm dimensions of arr
dim(arr)
```
Question #9
Answer:
When you run dim(arr), it outputs c(2, 3, 2). The three numbers represent the size of each dimension in order:
 
First number (2) — Number of Rows: Specifies how many horizontal rows are in each layer/matrix slice.
Second number (3) — Number of Columns: Specifies how many vertical columns are in each layer/matrix slice.
Third number (2) — Number of Layers/Slices: Specifies how many 2D matrices are stacked together along the 3rd dimension.
 
Question #10
Answer:
Real-World Example:
 
Student Exam Scores Across Multiple Semesters.
Rows: Individual Students (e.g., Ana, Ben).
Columns: Subjects / Quizzes (e.g., Math, Science, English).
3rd Dimension (Layers): Semesters or Academic Years (e.g., Semester 1, Semester 2).
 
Why a single 2D matrix would not be enough:
A single 2D matrix can only record student scores for a single point in time (1 semester) across two axes (Students $\times$ Subjects). To track how each student performs across those same subjects across multiple semesters, you need a 3rd dimension to represent time without flattening or duplicating rows and columns into an unorganized grid.
 
Part F — Critical Thinking Challenge
```{r}
```{r}
# Define class_a and class_b
class_a <- matrix(c(85, 90, 78, 92), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                  dimnames = list(c("S1", "S2"), c("Midterm", "Final")))
 
class_b <- matrix(c(88, 84, 95, 91), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                  dimnames = list(c("S3", "S4"), c("Midterm", "Final")))
 
# Combine class_a and class_b into all_students
all_students <- rbind(class_a, class_b)
all_students
```
 
```{r}
# Compute each student's average score across Midterm and Final
rowMeans(all_students)
```
 
Question #11
Explain WHY you chose cbind() or rbind() in challenge-1.
What clue in the data (shared row names vs. shared column names) told you which function was correct?
 
Answer:
Function Choice: rbind() was used because we are adding new student observations (rows) to the dataset, not adding new exam subjects (columns).
Clue in the Data: Both matrices share identical column names ("Midterm" and "Final"), but have distinct row names ("S1", "S2" vs. "S3", "S4"). Since rbind() requires matching column names/dimensions to stack rows on top of each other, sharing column names was the key indicator to use rbind().
 
Question #12
Suppose instead of 2 classes you had 5 classes, each recorded as a separate matrix with the same 2 columns (Midterm, Final).
Describe, in plain language (no code required), how you would combine all 5 into a single matrix, and how you would check your final result is correct using dim().
 
Answer:
How to Combine: You would pass all 5 matrices into rbind() in a single call (e.g., rbind(class_1, class_2, class_3, class_4, class_5)), which stacks all class matrices vertically into one master matrix.
 
How to Check using dim(): Run dim() on the final combined matrix.
The number of columns (the 2nd dimension) should still be 2 (corresponding to "Midterm" and "Final").
The number of rows (the 1st dimension) should equal the total sum of all students across all 5 classes combined.
 
Conclusion
In 3–4 sentences, summarize the key differences between a matrix and an array, and describe a situation where cbind()/rbind() would be useful in a real dataset you might work with.
 
Answer:
A matrix is strictly a two-dimensional data structure consisting of rows and columns, whereas an array generalizes this structure into $N$ dimensions by allowing three or more dimensions to be stacked together. In practice, rbind() is essential when appending new records over time, such as adding a new batch of monthly customer survey results as extra rows to an existing dataset. Conversely, cbind() is ideal for appending new calculated metrics or variables, such as binding a newly calculated "total score" column alongside existing test scores. Together, these functions provide flexible tools for dynamically updating real-world tabular data without altering the core structure.
